title: Maine's Senate Race Tests Whether Voters Still Care About Collins' Kavanaugh Vote
summary: In Maine, a state where women make up the majority of the population, Senator Susan Collins is running for a sixth term. Her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court is casting a long shadow. That vote was crucial: Kavanaugh was confirmed 50-48, and he later joined the 6-3 conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Since then, abortion has been banned in much of the United States. This is the first time Collins has been on the ballot since that ruling. For voters like Erin Evans, 56, of Portland, that's a betrayal. For years, Planned Parenthood's endorsement of Collins persuaded Evans to vote for her, believing the moderate Republican would protect abortion access. Now she says she is "just furious with myself" for those votes. She's backing Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger trying to deny Collins a sixth term. "I was a really uninformed voter," Evans said. "I thought any woman from Maine was probably in line with me." Both candidates are appealing to women, who vote at a slightly higher rate than men in Maine. Democrats are spending big to remind voters of Collins' Kavanaugh vote. An advocacy group called Affordable Maine has spent nearly $10 million on ads about Collins and other Trump-appointed judges who oppose abortion. Planned Parenthood Votes has spent at least $500,000 on similar ads. An additional $32 million has been spent by Win Senate, a political action committee focused on Collins. But Collins has a 30-year record of winning, even as Maine voters have rejected Republican presidential nominees since 1988. And the abortion issue trails others in importance. In 2020, 76% of Maine voters in the Senate race said the Supreme Court should not overturn Roe, including most Collins voters. Yet 35% of her supporters wanted Roe overturned. Collins has said she does not regret her Kavanaugh vote, and she criticized the 2022 decision. Some voters, like Democrat Mary Ann Lynch, still support her. "Neither party, in my view, has a monopoly on the truth," Lynch said. The election is November 3.
why_it_matters: This race tests whether a single Supreme Court confirmation vote can still end a 30-year political career — and whether abortion remains a decisive issue for American voters now that states, rather than courts, write the rules.

background_read: Susan Collins (a Republican who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate since 1997) is one of the last remaining moderate Republicans in Congress, known for occasionally breaking with her party.

Brett Kavanaugh (the Supreme Court justice President Trump nominated in 2018) was confirmed after hearings dominated by allegations of sexual assault, which he denied; his vote was crucial to the court's 6-3 conservative majority.

Roe v. Wade (the 1973 Supreme Court decision that made abortion legal nationwide) was overturned in 2022 in a case called Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which sent the rules back to individual states.

Planned Parenthood (a national health organization that provides reproductive care, including abortion, and supports abortion rights) had endorsed Collins in past races — which is why some voters feel personally misled.

Maine is a small New England state with an unusual political tradition: it has elected moderate Republicans for decades and has not backed a Republican for president since 1988. Outside money now dominates its Senate races, because since the Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United decision, political action committees can raise and spend unlimited amounts.

perspectives.description: Collins has won in Maine for three decades even as the state rejected Republican presidential nominees, and supporters like Mary Ann Lynch praise her independence, saying neither party has a monopoly on the truth. Her campaign argues voters judge her whole record, not one vote.

Voters who trusted Collins' moderate image say they feel betrayed, because her Kavanaugh vote was decisive in building the majority that overturned Roe. Outside groups are spending millions of dollars to make sure Mainers remember that vote at the ballot box.

The polling cuts both ways: in 2020, 76% of Maine Senate-race voters opposed overturning Roe, but 35% of Collins supporters wanted it overturned, and abortion ranks below other issues for many voters. Collins has also criticized the 2022 ruling while refusing to regret her confirmation vote.

November 3 will show whether the Kavanaugh vote still defines Collins now that abortion policy has moved from the courts to state legislatures. The result will help decide how much weight a single confirmation vote carries in future Senate races.
